query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In the as‐cast, single‐phase AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy, intermediate-temperature thermal aging triggers a nanoscale phase separation that leads to the formation of brittle precipitates. These precipitates, located at grain boundaries and/or within grains, mediate a change in fracture behavior by promoting crack nucleation and growth under load, resulting in a macroscopic transition from ductile to brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: as-cast, single-phase AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy with high toughness and ductility
generation.intervention: Application of intermediate-temperature thermal aging treatments, including both embrittlement-inducing and subsequent recovery treatments
generation.conditions: Thermal aging at intermediate temperatures under service-relevant conditions, with comparisons made between untreated, embrittled, and recovery-treated samples
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale brittle precipitates (potential intermetallic phases) that form at grain boundaries and possibly within grains
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging induces local compositional fluctuations in the complex studied alloy, leading to nanoscale phase separation. The emergent brittle precipitates act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, thus reducing toughness. Recovery treatments can partially reverse this segregation and precipitate formation, restoring ductility. This mechanism distinctly differs from conventional alloy embrittlement where grain-boundary segregation and coarse precipitation dominate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to intermediate-temperature aging will exhibit measurable reductions in fracture toughness and increased brittleness relative to the as-cast baseline. Recovery-treated samples should show improved toughness compared to the embrittled samples, but may not fully reach the ductility of the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, single-phase HEA state with high toughness and ductility
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under intermediate-temperature aging conditions relevant to service environments and under mechanical loadings that promote crack propagation; behavior might differ at extreme temperatures or under different strain rates.
generation.uncertainty: The precise volume fraction, spatial distribution, and exact crystallographic nature of the nanoscale precipitates remain uncertain, as does the quantitative relationship between precipitate density and toughness reduction.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of samples: (1) untreated as-cast AlCoCrFeNi HEA, (2) samples aged at intermediate temperatures to induce embrittlement, and (3) samples aged under the same conditions followed by a recovery heat treatment aimed at re-dissolving precipitates. Characterize microstructure (using TEM, SEM, and XRD) for the presence and distribution of precipitates and perform mechanical tests (tensile, fracture toughness, and impact tests) under comparable service loading conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM imaging, and phase identification via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intermediate-temperature aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness or if microstructural characterization shows no formation of nanoscale brittle precipitates compared to the as-cast baseline, the hypothesis is falsified. In addition, if recovery treatments do not result in measurable improvement in toughness relative to the embrittled samples, the proposed mechanism would be questioned.
